blocks.text: The conservation of angular momentum plays an important part in shaping moving air patterns, together with the Earth's rotation. The angular momentum of an air mass about the Earth's axis is L = mvr, where m is the mass of the air, r its distance from the rotation axis and v its velocity. In atmospheric science we usually use the specific angular momentum, the angular momentum per unit mass: L = rv (21.6).

As air moves from the equator towards a pole it keeps its specific angular momentum. Its distance r from the axis decreases, so its eastward speed v must increase to keep rv constant. The ground beneath moves east more slowly at higher latitudes, so this air moves east faster than the surface: seen from the ground it is deflected towards the east, which is to the right in the northern hemisphere. Air moving from a pole towards the equator does the opposite: it lags behind the faster-moving ground and is deflected westwards, again to the right of its motion in the northern hemisphere. This apparent deflection of moving air by the Earth's rotation is the Coriolis effect: to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere. It does not change the speed of the air but changes its path, creating curved wind patterns.

blocks.title: Poleward air moves ahead, not behind
blocks.text: The book says that air moving from the equator towards a pole 'lags behind the rotation of the surface beneath it'. By its own argument (r decreases, so v increases), poleward-moving air moves eastward faster than the ground beneath it, so it gets ahead and is deflected east; it is air moving towards the equator that lags behind. In both cases the deflection is to the right in the northern hemisphere.

These deflected air flows form three distinct atmospheric circulation cells in each hemisphere: the Hadley cell, the Ferrel cell and the Polar cell (Fig 21.14). In the Hadley cell, warm air rises at the equator, flows towards the poles at height and sinks near 30 degrees latitude; in the Polar cell, cold air sinks at the poles and rises near 60 degrees; the Ferrel cell lies between them. Near the surface, the Coriolis effect turns the returning flows into the trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies.

On its right edge, loops in each hemisphere show three cells: the Hadley cell (red) between 0 and 30 degrees, the Ferrel cell (green) between 30 and 60 degrees and the Polar cell (purple) between 60 and 90 degrees. Text explains where air rises and sinks and that the Coriolis effect turns the surface flows into the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

blocks.long_description: Heat from the equator is carried poleward in three steps rather than one big loop, because the Coriolis effect turns the flow before it can travel all the way from the equator to the pole.

blocks.prompt: Which way is moving air deflected in the southern hemisphere, and why?
blocks.explanation: To the left of its motion, because of the Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect, from conservation of angular momentum); in the northern hemisphere it is deflected to the right.

items: Specific angular momentum L = rv is conserved by moving air.
Coriolis effect: deflection to the right (north) and left (south); speed unchanged.
Three cells per hemisphere: Hadley (0-30), Ferrel (30-60), Polar (60-90).
